etymologies.etymologyHTML: Possibly from Middle English fit (“an adversary of equal power”), of uncertain further origin. The original sense appears to have been "to marshal or deploy troops", which shifted to "to suit (troops to a certain location" > "suitable", and may be further related to Icelandic fitja (“to web, knit, cast on”).

definitions.definition: Suitable; proper

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Job 34:18:
quote.text: Is it fit to say a king, Thou art wicked?

quote.citation: 1902, John Buchan, The Outgoing of the Tide:
quote.text: He had drunk more than was fit for him, and he was singing some light song, when he saw approaching, as he said, the pale horse mentioned in the Revelation, with Death seated as the rider.

quote.citation: 2005, Lesley Brown, Sophist, translation of original by Plato, 243d:
quote.text: The rest we'll leave to be examined later, if we think fit;

quote.citation: 2015 February 1, Howard Tayler, Schlock Mercenary‎[1], archived from the original on 14 May 2024:
quote.text: Sergeant Schlock has no horse, no armor, and no sword, but even the mightiest Mongol horse-warrior would see in him a fit heir.

definitions.definition: Adapted to a purpose or environment.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: That which ordinary men are fit for, I am qualified in.

definitions.definition: In good shape; physically well.
(British, informal, chiefly slang) Sexually attractive; good-looking; fanciable.

quote.citation: 2004, Mike Skinner (lyrics and music), “Fit but You Know It”, in A Grand Don't Come for Free, performed by The Streets:
quote.text: I think you are really fit / You're fit but my gosh don't you know it.

quote.citation: 2007, “Foundations”, in Kate Nash, Paul Eppworth (lyrics), Made of Bricks, performed by Kate Nash:
quote.text: I said I'd rather be with your friends, mate, cos they are much fitter.

definitions.definition: Prepared; ready.

quote.citation: 1600, [Torquato Tasso], “(please specify |book=1 to 20)”, in Edward Fairefax [i.e., Edward Fairfax], transl., Godfrey of Bulloigne, or The Recouerie of Ierusalem. […], London:  […]  Ar[nold] Hatfield, for I[saac] Iaggard and M[atthew] Lownes, →OCLC:
quote.text: So fit to shoot, she singled forth among her foes who first her quarry's strength should feel.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To be suitable for.

quote.citation: 1918, Richard Dennis Teall Hollister, Speech-making, publ. George Wahr, pg. 81:
quote.text: The speaker should be certain that his subject fits the occasion.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To have sufficient space available at some location to be able to be there.
(transitive) To conform to in size and shape.
(intransitive) To be of the right size and shape

quote.citation: 2001, “Schism”, in Maynard James Keenan (lyrics), Adam Jones, Danny Carey, Maynard James Keenan, and Justin Chancellor (music), Lateralus, performed by Tool, track 5:
quote.text: I know the pieces fit / 'Cause I watched them fall away

quote.citation: 2016 February 2, Kate Winslet et al., Jimmy Kimmel Live!‎[2]:
quote.text: Even though in a way you let him freeze to death in the water, because the way I see it...I agree. Y'know, I think he actually could have fitted on that bit of door.There was plenty of room on the raft.I know. I know, I know.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To tailor; to change to the appropriate size.
(transitive, with to) To make conform in size and shape.
(transitive) To be in agreement with.

quote.citation: 2004 October 14, Don Ringe, “Old English maþelian, mæþlan, mǣlan”, in J. H. W. Penney, editor, Indo-European Perspectives: Studies in Honour of Anna Morpurgo Davies‎[3], Oxford University Press, →ISBN, page 427:
quote.text: Type D half-lines ending in words of this type are analysed by Hutcheson as ending in two completely unstressed syllables. That analysis must be descriptively correct for, say, the 10th cent.; whether it would have fitted the facts in the 8th cent. is much less clear.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To adjust.
(transitive) To attach, especially when requiring exact positioning or sizing.

quote.citation: 2012 May 13, Andrew Benson, “Williams's Pastor Maldonado takes landmark Spanish Grand Prix win”, in BBC Sport‎[4]:
quote.text: Williams had a problem fitting his left rear tyre and that left Alonso only 3.1secs adrift when he rejoined from his final stop three laps later.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To equip or supply.
(transitive) To make ready.

quote.citation: 1871, Florence Nightingale, Una and the Lion, page 12:
quote.text: Thirty years ago, if a girl wished for training, there was none to be had. I can truly say there was no training to be had to fit a woman thoroughly for any life whatever.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To be seemly.
To be proper or becoming.

quote.citation: 1725, Homer, “Book III”, in [Alexander Pope], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], volume I, London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: Nor fits it to prolong the heav'nly feast.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be in harmony.
The degree to which something fits.
Conformity of elements one to another.
The part of an object upon which anything fits tightly.
(advertising) Measure of how well a particular commercial execution captures the character or values of a brand.
(statistics) Goodness of fit.
(bridge) The quality of a partnership's combined holding of cards in a suit, particularly of trump.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Unknown, possibly from Old English fitt (“song”), or from the sense of fitted to length. Compare Old Saxon *fittea (attested in the borrowed Latin vittea).

definitions.definition: (archaic) A section of a poem or ballad.

quote.citation: 1771, Samuel Johnson, "Letter to Bennet Langton, Esq. (March 20)," in James Boswell, Life of Samuel Johnson (1791), vol 2:
quote.text: Dr. Percy has written a long ballad in many fits.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Unknown, possibly from Old English fitt (“conflict”). Compare Cornish fit (“game match, bout”); or else, probably cognate with Italian fitta (“pain, especially sudden and stabbing pain”). See more at Latin fīgere.

definitions.definition: A seizure or convulsion.
(medicine) A sudden and vigorous appearance of a symptom over a short period of time.
A sudden outburst of emotion.
A sudden burst (of an activity).

quote.citation: 2007 July 9, Ryan J. Foley, “Wisconsin city's largest employer threatens to leave over ethanol”, in Associated Press:
quote.text: A fit of spring-cleaning led Eric Brooks to a box of old newspaper clips from 1997.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, medicine) To suffer a fit.

quote.citation: 2016 May 18, “Three dogs die and seven more ill after drinking from the same Kent lake amid contamination fears”, in The Telegraph:
quote.text: A spokesman said: "It is believed they (the dogs) got into the lake and drank from it. They came out and started fitting. Shortly after that three of them died and vets are attempting to resuscitate the other one."

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Formed from fight on the model of bite:bit and light:lit.

definitions.definition: (African-American Vernacular, Southern US, dated) simple past and past participle of fight; fought.

quote.citation: 1867 November, unknown author, The Galaxy, volume 4, New York: W.C. & F.P. Church, retrieved 2023-10-27, page 883:
quote.text: There wonst was two cats in Kilkenny;  And aich thought there was one cat too many.    So they quarrelled and fit;    And they scratched, and they bit;     Till, excepting their tails      And some scraps of their nails,  Instead of two cats there wan't any.

quote.citation: c. 19th century, unknown author, Joshua Fit the Battle of Jericho
quote.text: Joshua fit the battle of Jericho and the walls came tumbling down

quote.citation: a. 1940, Mildred Haun, “Shin-Bone Rocks”, in The Hawk's Done Gone, page 218:
quote.text: He didn't just set around and try to out sweettalk[sic] somebody; he got out and out-fit somebody.  He wouldn't be blowing when he told his boys how he fit for the woman he got.

definitions.definition: (slang) An outfit, a set of clothing.
